review:
The Bureau: XCOM Declassified was not well received by mainstream reviewers, but I personally enjoyed it a lot. Overall, it feels like a stripped down version of Mass Effect, but the combat stands out above other cover shooters. The game has a lot of flaws, but I encountered no bugs in the core game. The Hangar 6 DLC, however, would freeze briefly every few seconds and rendered the game nearly unplayable. 

The Bureau's combat puts you in control of William Carter, a rather generic protagonist with a gravelly voice. Conversations in the game are carried out with a radial menu lifted directly from Mass Effect. The dialogue isn't terribly interesting, and some of the characters facial animations appeared to not actually be finished. Their mouths move with odd robotic motions, and their eyes look eerily dead. Carter himself, and some of the other core characters have much better, albeit repetitive animations. The story is forgettable overall, but moves the game on well enough. It doesn't come anywhere close to the likes of Mass Effect though, and the fact that the developers chose to base their game design so heavily on Mass Effect is unfortunate given the weak story. Even still, the combat made the experience worthwhile.

Combat in the Bureau is at it's core a cover shooter in the vein of Mass Effect or Gears of War. It also gives you a pair of squadmates and allows you to give direct orders to them. The rookies you start with only have one or two abilities, as well as a command to focus on a specific target, and move to a location. Choosing where to move your squadmates is where the game gets a lot of it's strategic depth. You have to take into account how long they'll be exposed for, how far the nearest ally is if they need a revive, where the enemies are, how much protection the cover offers, and how easily they can use their abilities from their location. Overall it makes for a far more interesting experience than your standard cover shooter. Abilities range from dropping mines, shield domes, artillery strikes, and others.

The combat isn't perfect though. Your squadmates seem to move into stupid locations occasionally, either exposing themselves to unnecessary fire, going down somewhere difficult to revive them, or both. It's not quite clear why this happens, but it doesn't happen very often at least. The encounters feel somewhat repetitive, but they ramp up in difficulty at a good rate. The weapons are fairly standard for a cover shooter; human and alien variations of the standard rifle, pistol, sniper and so on. Enemies on the other hand provide a bit more variety, healing their allies, granting them shields, spawning new enemies, or even mind controlling your squadmates.

The graphics generally look good, with a variety of scenes ranging from idyllic small towns to metallic alien structures. Some elements though stand out like a sore thumb. An ugly low res skybox in one of the first scenes of the game is jarringly bad to look at in stark contrast to the cutscene that precedes it. Other elements like a destroyed tank with an ugly texture and a low poly model, or the abyss below an alien tower filled with an ugly brown fog that would have been acceptable years ago, but looks disappointing today. The rest of the game, however, especially the weapon reload animations look and sound good.

The Bureau's worst offense however, is sure to be a dealbreaker for some fans of the mainstream XCOM games. The only thing The Bureau has in common with XCOM itself is the aliens and the weapon types. Unlocking new weapons is done merely by picking them up off the ground rather than researching them. Dying only puts you back to the latest checkpoint, and while you can lose squadmates permanently if they bleed out in some difficulty settings, I'm fairly sure if you die yourself they'll be back with you at the last checkpoint. 

By removing research, permadeath, and forcing the player down a linear path, I'm sure some players will deem the game unworthy of the XCOM title. While these issues did grate on me at first, it was the combat that kept me playing and enjoying every minute of it. Even though the story is just average, it isn't particularly time consuming like it is in Mass Effect. While I feel the game could have played more to it's strengths, it was still well worth the time and money while on sale. I wouldn't hesitate to reccomend this game to fans of Mass Effect, though fans of the classic XCOM games or Enemy Unknown will not enjoy it unless they also enjoy a good cover shooter.

This was a decent game in my opinion. I think most people don't understand that they were trying something new. They were not trying to be XCOM: Enemy Unknown. It is very similar in play style to the first Mass Effect game. It is basically just a story that tries to add dept to the XCOM lore and show that they have been active for a long time. Not a great game, but not deserving of all the hate.

The Bureau: XCOM Declassified isn't bad, it just isn't very good. It's a bit threadbare, feeling like several incomplete ideas that have been rushed out the gate.

Realistically, I suspect The Bureau was completed on a small-ish budget after lingering around in development hell for a few years. Something about the game makes it feel like it's ten years or more old, if it wasn't for some of the DirectX 11 effects looking so sparkly it'd be easy to think it was from the early 2000's. Many of the locations are bare and empty places, feeling like they've been built in a rush, and often with several such vacant sets stitched together without any combat or events to distract, assumably to give the impression of covering a lot of ground in a mission. Other areas have clearly had some time and attention spent on them, and the locations and missions waver back-and-forth on this attention / quality scale, leaving the experience feeling quite jarring. You'll wander from a well-realised street, strewn with debris, bodies and signs of previous life... into an area that feels like it's been imported from a PS2 game.

The mechanics of the game basically play out like Mass Effect's combat, or Mass Effect 3 more specifically. It's a cover-based shooter where you run around with two squadmates, you have abilities with cooldowns, can issue orders and give movement directions to your squad. Enemies come in multiple varieties, some with shields and some with armour, with a few enemy types creating interesting tactical choices (a unit that supplies shields to all other nearby units, for example, if taken out the shields drop and make the fight easier). Unfortunately, where Mass Effect shines in making you care for your squad, here they are just flat cardboard bodies waiting for you to pull their puppet strings. They also keep respawning in front of you whenever you cross through a 'loading door' (frequent area transitions where the game loads the next section as your character very slowly opens a door and looks left and right before giving you control again), which is a bit distracting.

In fact, I felt the game lacked polish in general. I fell through the level geometry and died twice in eight hours of play, once whilst just running down a straight corridor. Audio logs can be found and played, although walking away from them they fade until inaudible (if I have to stand still to listen to them, they may as well be written text!). The controls aren't terrible, but movement feels clunky and stiff, for example; when you run there is absolutely no strafing, not even in a limited fashion, leaving you to clumsily course-correct with your mouse as you charge forward. You also tend to pop in and out of cover randomly at times, especially if strafing in cover, and controlling your squadmates feels awkward (fortunately the game slows down time during this).

Much of the story is told over radio as you run between fights, although there are some cutscenes that deal with exposition. The game also uses a dialogue wheel, just like the Mass Effect series, allowing you to choose between being vaguely rude or agreeable, it's a nice enough touch, although it felt a bit redundant with such small scope for actual meaningful choice. Levels are basically linear paths that open into combat arenas, the main missions last 30 to 60 minutes each, with side missions from 15 to 30 minutes roughly (I only did a couple, they felt fairly pointless). The game isn't overly long with six main missions, the story is mildly amusing with some interesting characters (although the main player character really started to grate on me). The plot felt like it tried to raise the stakes too high a number of times implying that Earth has basically been wiped out and already lost by the midway point of the game, then later claiming it's not as bad as implied, which breaks the suspension of disbelief somewhat.

Imbetween the missions, the game flirts with the idea of being an XCOM-style strategy game where you pick missions and kit out your squad, but with only six main plot missions and (I believe) seven side-quest 'minor missions', it doesn't feel like there's a lot of variety or choice. The equipment feels limited, with only a handful of weapons to equip and the only other equipment slot being a 'backpack' which acts as a kind of modifier for ammo, health regen, or ability cooldowns.

Overall, not a bad game, just not a particularly good one. It feels like it didn't succeed at being the mixture of genres it wanted to be, and it's not particularly good at being any ONE genre either. The plot is so-so, and the clunky and unpolished feel doesn't help. But if you don't mind all this and want a simple squad and cover-based shooter, this might entertain.

The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is a sci-fi squad-based tactical third-person shooter developed by 2K Marin and published by 2K Games. After a devastating surprise attack by a hostile otherworldly lifeform cripples defense and communication networks across the planet, F.B.I. Agent William Carter suddenly finds himself enlisted into The Bureau. A top-secret government organization originally tasked with responding to a communistic occupation of America but now tasked with defending the Earth from an even greater alien threat. As Agent Carter it will be up to you to issue commands while leading your squad through intense tactical combat as you set off on what may be the most important missions ever handed down in your attempt to repel an alien invasion and save humanity from enslavement and possible extinction. Welcome to The Bureau.

Prior to this I had never played an XCOM game before but was enlightened enough to know that they were tactical turn-based titles and immediately realized that this particular game seemed to step outside of that box. If I had to compare the gameplay of The Bureau: XCOM Declassified to anything then the first games that come to mind would be the "Mass Effect" trilogy. If you are at all familiar with those titles then you will feel right at home with the gameplay of The Bureau as the squad-based tactical combat, third person shooter elements and even the dialogue in the cutscenes are very reminescent of "Mass Effect" which is not a bad thing as I completely loved that franchise myself. The gameplay isn't as polished as "Mass Effect" but a nice try nonetheless. I found the combat of The Bureau to be alot of fun as you have the opportunity to pause the action while you issue a number of orders to your squad like where to take cover and what abilities/tactics to use as you attempt to take complete command and control of the battlefield. Speaking of which, the battles are quite challenging as you will often find yourselves drastically outnumbered by a technologically superior force but if you strategize and manage your team effectively victory will always be within your grasp and for me this is where the gameplay of this title truly shines. Proper management of your team and where to place them as well as who to hit and where to move to next is essential in maintaining a victorious campaign so if you're someone who doesn't like to micro-manage everything your squad does then this probably isn't a game for you? Also, there are R.P.G. elements incorporated as you earn experience and level up your team giving you access to new skills and perks which will further increase your squads combat effectiveness. Additionally, I found the amount of customization enticing in that you can tailor your squad right down to the most miniscule of things such as the color of their clothing and even their names. You also have the option to select the loadout that they take into battle as far as which types of weapons and packs as well as the specializations of the troopers themselves like recon, engineer, support or commando. Moving on to the narrative, I found the story of this game to be another one of it's best features what with me being a big science fiction fan I never tire of the tried and true "alien invasion" theme and this title handles it marvelously. The storyline kept me intrigued from the beginning to the very end as you learn more about The Bureau as well as the intentions of the alien force. With all the positive attributes that this game has I must mention one GLARING flaw and that is the HORRIBLY unstable nature of this title. Throughout my playthrough I found myself constantly assaulted with glitches ranging from random crashes, unforgivable stuttering at certain points in game thank you very much PhysX and the sound cutting out which all required me to restart. This soon became quite frustrating especially when you're right in the middle of a battle or a pivotal moment in the game. Nevertheless, even with these terrible technical problems I never let them detract from my enjoyment of this excellent title...glitches withstanding. To sum things up, despite some rather overbearing technical issues I found the fascinating story, wonderful squad-based tactical combat and R.P.G. elements of The Bureau: XCOM Declassified to be a very entertaining experience.

Visually I found this title to be most impressive as the game has gorgeous textures, makes use of a beautiful color palette as well as depth of field/particle effects, terrific lighting and outstanding sound quality. The animation is also very good especially on the N.P.C.'s and various other background objects in the game as well as the aliens themselves. Also of note is when you are transitioning from one area to another like when your squad enters for example a warehouse...Carter pans the room back and forth with his weapon as he checks it for hostiles which is quite an immersive little detail that I enjoyed watching. Animation-wise, one other thing that I would like to mention is something that I tend to notice alot whenever I play third person games and that is the handling of doors. This may seem like a small unimportant detail to most but I take notice when a game has a character actually push open, press a button or manipulate a handle in order to open a door rather than just stand there and have it magically open even though your character made no effort to do so. It constantly shocks me how games like "The Witcher" were doing this back in 2008 while I continue to see big budget titles to this day drop the ball on door opening animations...I could name many names right now but will refrain from doing so. Thankfully, this title does an exceptional job of this and deserves praise for it. As far as the overall presentation of this title goes, I really enjoyed the 1960's theme with the music, clothing, speech and vehicles among many other things and believe it or not it contrasted quite well against the futuristic and very high tech aspect of the alien invasion force. As far as I know, we don't often see games set in or around this time period so this was quite a nice gaming experience visually. In summary, The Bureau: XCOM Declassified provided a terrific looking visual escapade through a rather significant historical period of time in this world.

This game sat in my inventory for years but thankfully turned out to be one of those "hidden gem" titles as I thoroughly enjoyed my playthrough of The Bureau: XCOM Declassified. It's a shame that the game was, from what I read, a commercial failure and received so much hate from the XCOM enthusiasts but I'm guessing that my lack of having played any other XCOM titles prior to this allowed me to be a little more forgiving and un-biased in this situation so who knows? It's a great game and my only complaints are the glitches and that it's fairly short in length. As options go, there is D.L.C. in the form of "Code Breakers", "Hanger 6 R&D" and "Light Plasma Pistol" which are basically two additional missions and a new weapon added to the base game. There are also Steam Achievements and Steam Trading Cards to collect. In conclusion, if you can stomach the constant technical problems with the game and yes there will be many...I found The Bureau: XCOM Declassified with it's excellent tactical combat and thrilling "David versus Goliath" style invasion story really enticing and would HIGHLY RECOMMEND this title to tactical, strategy and story-rich adventure fans.

I've been going back and playing all my "old school" games from better times. It's amazing how "average" games and movies from the Olden Times are literally masterpieces compared to the absolute slop we get served up now. 

This is a fun little lore ad on for the Xcom games, nothing earth shattering, but a solid story and light tactical shooter where you can order your squad mates. Def worth the 3 bucks or so it regularly goes on sale for.

The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is a budget Mass Effect clone set in the rebooted XCOM universe. It is a prequel taking place in 1962 in which an alien invasion occurs but is somehow covered up enough that there is no mention of it by the time the second invasion occurs during Enemy Unknown. The game was originally announced in 2006 and went through several variations with mixed reception and development hell until the final product was released in 2013. 

The Bureau is a third person shooter that mixes squad and power elements from the original Mass Effect while using design language to keep it in line with Enemy Unknown. For the most part it works and I never got bored throughout my playthrough. The downside is that both the enemy and ally AI is mediocre at best making some battles a slog due to your squad getting themselves killed by charging for zero reason. The weapon variety is also not very memorable and could have been improved if they had implemented some sort of research or upgrade tree like in Enemy Unknown. 

The story has its ups and downs as a mixture of the X-Files, 1950s Sci-Fi B-movies, and The Right Stuff. The story starts out strong but then things start to happen as you go from mission to mission but does not adequately explain why or how much time has passed. There is not really any clear narrative until near the end when the war is coming to a close. The characters are not very memorable and the dialogue options are meaningless. There are several sidequests and dialogue trees in this game but they pretty much do nothing and have no narrative consequence. None have any impact on characterization or the ending and you can really just do all the main line missions if you want to and miss absolutely nothing in importance. 

I actually enjoyed my time playing this game despite its glaring flaws. There really is not anything else like it on the market and if anything it is an enjoyable romp of a retro scifi war of the worlds film from the early cold war era. If you liked XCOM and are not turned off by the vastly different gameplay then this might be worth a shot for you.

The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is a story about the struggles A Good Game encounters while it desperately tries to escape the clutches of its evil stepmother, A Bad Game.

The Bureau is a tactical third person, cover based shooter that takes place during the 1960s in the United States.  You play as William Carter, an agent with the CIA, and command 2 other soldiers as you fight off an alien invasion.  The main draw of the tactical portion is the "Battle Focus" where you slow down time to give orders to your agents, executing movements and plans. There's some light RPG elements that accompany it, where you maintain a small roster of fellow agents and level them up, picking up abilities as they progress through the levels. 

Let's talk about the evil stepmother!

Even when you ignore the XCOM stuff, the story is a mess (XCOM fans, read below, but spoilers beware).  It's very generic sc-fi stuff, but it suffers from some weird pacing and organization issues.  The characters have no personality to them, they're just scarecrows with voiceboxes.  Obviously, the bulk of the game is spent fighting, but even that has its issues.  The squad AI can act pretty wonky, and they require a fair bit of micromanagement.  Multiple times, especially towards the end of the game, I would watch one of my squadmembers try and fire at something below him and achieve nothing more than hammer the window ledge for a minute straight.  Enemy grenades are aplenty, and your squad members do a good job of diving out of the way, but this leads to issues whenever they dive into the corner right next to the grenade or decide to charge through enemy fire to get another piece of cover.  I was pretty active with assigning targets and using abilities, but in the beginning I was still scoring 95% of the kills myself.  As your agents advance through the ranks, they get more abilities which help them carry their own weight, but they don't become much handier with a gun.  

The squad management stuff is also frustratingly vague- when you recruit a new agent, you can pick a background for them that gives some sort of passive bonus, but the game doesn't give any hard figures as to what it does.  You get a blurb, so maybe you'll get a vague idea of what the bonus confers, but sometimes you don't even get that.  This is also a problem with equipment.  Your agents get two pieces of equipment, a weapon and a backpack, and the backpack features a description of what it does but never gives hard values, and a lot of them seem to do the same thing.  For example, you'll find mulitple backpacks that reduce incoming damage, but a lot of these offer bonuses on top of reducing damage, but there's one backpack that only reduces damage.  Does it reduce more damage?  Who knows!

All this aside, there is a shiny nugget of Good Game underneath it all.  There's a small bright spot in the story that probably lasts for about 20 minutes or so towards the end that was waaaaay more interesting than anything else that had happened so far, but then they decide to throw it away and keep on marching ahead.  The Battle Focus portion has some control issues, but overall I was really impressed with the way plans were executed.  The agent creation system was really interesting, as well, and it was a shame that it didn't offer much more depth or give you much of a reason to use more agents.  I'm convinced that there's good ideas sprinkled about the game like breadcrumbs, and if someone could follow it, there'd be something beautiful at the end.

I still had fun with the game, despite a long list of complaints.  At its core, it's a solid, if unremarkable, third person cover shooter.  While I have no desire to ever replay the game, and I'm going to uninstall it after this, I certainly don't feel as it was a waste of my time.  I would never encourage something to buy it, but I'd never discourage someone from buying it, either.

What I paid for it: 12.50
What I would pay for it: 10.00

Everything in the review is based off of playing it on Veteran difficulty.

FOR XCOM FANS:

As an XCOM title, the game fails miserably, both from a narrative and mechanical sense.  From a narrative sense, my first complaint is that XCOM is an international effort. I get that the game is a tie in, but I don't think I ever heard once the justification of why the organization is called XCOM.  The actual name of the organization is "Bureau of Operations and Command", and then they just start calling it XCOM.  There's also the timeline issue.  The game takes place in 1962, and during the course of the game you get all sorts of crazy, alien technology.  In 1999/2015, when the aliens come back, instead of just shipping over the technology/knowledge on how to beat them, I have to watch my Squaddies die brutal deaths all over the globe because the Air Force lost a Laser SMG in warehouse?  The Council only gets the barest of nods- if you have subtitles on, during the ending scene, someone with the name "Councilman" speaks.  Which, honestly, could just be a happy accident.

Granted, a lot of this can be handwaved away with the word "Spin-off", which is fine.  They pretty obviously co-opted Sectoids into this, but if you were to remove them and all instances of the word XCOM, this would be unrecognizable as an XCOM title.  Which takes us to how the game fails XCOM mechanically.

XCOM, for the most part, has been a game about overcoming insurmountable odds and crafting your own stories as you play through a game.  Yes, there may have been a Squaddie O'Malley in other people's games, but only [i]your[/i] Squaddie O'Malley managed to kill two Chryssalids in a warehouse by himself before meeting his untimely end to panic induced friendly fire during the next mission.

The Bureau strips all that out.  Between the fact that soldiers are incredibly hard to lose- once they go down, there's a bleed out period where they die if they're not revived but you have plenty of time to bring them up. Between that, and the game focusing on characters that already exist, you just don't care about your agents. I still know the name of the 6 soldiers who went on my last Temple Ship Assault, but I couldn't even tell you the name of one of my agents from the game.  They were just "Level 5 Sniper I" and "Level 5 Engineer II".  By removing any tension, and making the player character a tough, disaffected badass who growls more than talks, it just turns into a shootbang gallery where fancy special effects happen sometimes rather than a tense, careful advance against enemies who are far more powerful than you.

If you came here for an XCOM title, I'd advise you to keep looking.

Short review:
If you want to babysit some agents through linear, scripted cover based firefights to crawl your way through an ok story, which was developed as a misguided attempt to enlarge the XCom-franchise, this game might just be the thing for you. If any of this raised a warning sign for you, better keep away, there are a plenty better games you can spend your time and money on.

Thorough review:

The good parts:
The game is definitely not completely bad. The perk system is nice, you can work your way up to some nice combos to make a way out of a tough situation, or wreck your enemies, which can feel satisfying. The story seems kinda promising, though i can't say for sure, since it certainly wasn't enough to keep me hooked. And i think the visuals are quite good, in a way it manages to capture a "noirish-scifiy-actiony" feel, which can be an enticing mix. The sound is ok, nothing special.

The bad parts:
Overall, it's just not enough! The perk system is nice, this plus the squad & command system could make a fundament for a good strategy-shooter... but it just isn't. Since you can actively only control one squad member and the rest of the squad usually acts like the biggest morons you can imagine as "agents", it becomes incredibly difficult to just enjoy the action, while the command system becomes obligatory to keep your mates from killing themselves, i.e. you have to babysit them. All of this made the characters in this game, which are supposed to be more fleshed out a lot less interesting than the generic soldiers in "XCom:Enemy Unkown". And in a game from 2013, i definitely expect some better A.I., or a way to deal with what's there more effectively, but neither is given here.
Now add to this a very linear progression with scripted encounters and little varieties to approach them, but "use perks to set up enemies, shoot enemies", which became a boring task for me way too soon and what you get is a game with little things to play with and no motivation.
And though i didn't seem to encounter as many problems as some other people, the game lacks a lot of polish and can too easily bug out or crash on you.

Recommendation:
Well, if you really want to play it, for the niche it provides, or for the little addition it does to the XCom franchise, do as you please. If you want to play a good squad-based tactical game, grab something else, like XCom proper, Shadowrun, Fire Emblem, or Hard West. If you want to play a good squad-based shooter, you might want to check out the Rainbow-Six series (Ubisoft warning). If you want to play a pure shooter or strategy game, reorient yourself.

[h1] BETRAYAL! - Wait no. This isn't that bad [/h1]

This game was never going to be a runaway success, It’s design as a tactical action shooter left it firmly in the shadow of the unreleased X-com: Alliance. An FPS Squad shooter slated for 2001. But releasing this near simultaneously with Enemy Unknown was a detrimental mistake that buried this game.
Which is a shame, because its not bad- despite a few questionable design choices.

[h2] This doesn't make the best first impression [/h2]

Ahem. If you check out the steam discussions many will complain the AI is underwhelming, which it half-true. The companions are lobotomised, until you get them to level 5. Then they become responsive and more importantly have enough health to not immediately keel over & die to every encounter.
Any orders you direct to your squad are immediately carried out, they even change texture to illustrate they’re following your commands. Their actions are queued and each class has their own set of unique abilities all designed to synergise.
Support casts Disrupt, you use the ability levitate, then Recon uses Critical strike. 
Congrats!
You just killed everything except for a Muton or Sectopod. If you time it right.

Commands are done through a proto Fallout 4 VATS system where time slows down, and there is even a mass effect dialogue wheel for interacting with characters. It’s neat. 

The squad is limited just to three which sucks since the player counts as a unit.
Mind control is a late game action which really adds tactical variety. Deployable drones, Turrets and Silacoid’s all work surprisingly well.
The combat is satisfying once you level up your roster of companions. Don’t worry about the permadeath, you can simultaneously send new recruits off to do automated missions as you play which levels them up.
A Total party kill is easily replaceable with no disadvantage, just customise the new squad to look like the old.
By the mid game I didn’t need to micromanage my companions anymore, they could tank most things, the AI automatically avoids grenades to the point they’ll never be hit. It’s nice… You just have to get them to level 5 because the starting health pool and their lack of abilities really screws with the AI’s capability to dynamically react.
These soldiers were lobotomised in the early game, they do get better.

[h2] The difficulty is meaningless [/h2]

You will never fight more than two mutons until the final level, you will only encounter a maximum of two Sectopod’s, only a handful of optional side missions have Sectoid’s swam you on mass and the Outsiders and all their variants can be managed systematically. Difficulty has no bearing on the mechanics.
It just nerfs your abilities and turns everything into a bullet sponge if you raise it.
Whilst I completed it on Commander difficulty, I did replay a little bit on novice and the early game was more enjoyable. The spawns didn’t change, only the enemie’s health.
Call me old fashioned but a Muton shouldn’t have more health than a Sectopod, quadrupedal tank. But on commander oh boy they do.

"The Bureau: XCOM Declassified". There are three major aspects of the game to talk about.

For one, this game was created for XCOM fans, with an extra layer of associations from the 60's era. The player will see all the major events of an alien invasion on Earth, from the first contact to the last repel battle, which, by all standards, will unfold on an alien ship, from where the entire invasion is organized. Keen on the setting, the player will be able to examine in detail the sequential construction of the XCOM base, go over all its iconic locations, from the headquarters and medical unit to laboratories and workshops. The player will take part in the capture of aliens and in their interrogations (without vivisection). He will have to defend the base from a full-scale attack in one moment... All in the third-view perspective. If this is not a quality fan-service, then what else? Unfortunately, not all XCOM fans appreciated the change of genre from strategy to shooter, but for me personally, the Bureau in this aspect is a very successful project.

The second major part of this game is the story plot. The scenario. And, while it is the most subjective part in this very subjective game parsing, I'd say, it was not bad until the very end of the game. A rather trivial, but thorough, with some interest on the part of the player, story about the events of an alien invasion, with extensive motivation for the participants in the conflict - it seems that everything is going well. The player is going through the chain of events with the protagonist, agent Carter, he's making some decisions on his field missions and between them, he is building bonds between major characters, and then Boom! - they all are failing some basic logic checks, and then agent Carter is not a hero anymore, all the bonds are broken, and the player have to finish the last mission with another character. All of the late chain of events is a pure Spanish shame to me, and that is why the replayability of this game going to nil, especially from the players who really delve into what is happening and tries to empathize with the heroes of story. This case is worse than with Bioshock Infinite ending. If you understand me there.

However. There are many players who don't care about the XCOM franchise or the story in shooting games. Or there might be people who actually liked the story in all its twists - it is very subjective, right? So, finally, the core of the game, the third thing in this review, but the first one that you need to take into consideration with the question "Should I buy it and play it?" The gameplay.

And that is where I'll go for the opinions of other people - like there in Steam reviews, or on Metacritic, or somewhere else. If we check those reviews in general, not including empty "10/10" and "0/10" ratings, we'll see that most of the players have found "The Bureau: XCOM Declassified" as a very mediocre shooter. You see, the game is generally slow. Narrow corridor locations are mainly built so that in the course of the player’s movement to tell him a story, with the scenery that he goes through. At some intervals, this journey through locations will be interrupted by battles with aliens, usually based on the principle of "arena with several waves of opponents". A key gameplay feature of "The Bureau" is positional shootouts with a strong focus on using the shelters. And the player have to manage not a one, but three characters simultaneously: one directly and two "companions" with constant order line. Like "move there", "shoot in that alien", "use a shield" and so on. Three characters in real-time battles. Sure, you have something like "pause mode" to send your orders, but it is still a real-time shooting game. And your "companions" are made so bad, that they always need your help with every move. Otherwise, they start running along the most idiotic routes, for example, right through a crowd of opponents. With an understandable deplorable result. So, as a positional shooter with shelters and teammates, this game loses to most similar games, including mediocre (in gameplay mechanics) shooters like "Spec Ops the Line" or "Kane & Lynch". Not to mention the really complex games of the "Ghost Recon" level. What is even worse - the most basic shooter mechanic, i.e. shooting - is really bad there in Bureau. In most cases (except fighting armoured Mutons and Sectopods), you will not feel any impact of your shooting. There are no destructible shelters in the game - and this feature is the most basic in third-view shooters (TPS) with shelters. Even the very early title in that genre, "Kill/Switch", had some. And "The Bureau", based on the XCOM - lacks any.

So, finally, let's summarize. If you really like all that is XCOM, this one is the best shooter game in that franchise. However, you have to deal both with boredom and irritation, the same with the “story” walkthrough on the simplest difficulty, and when trying to save both your nerves and partners, at maximum difficulty.

The overall product quality rating is 6/10, but for me - the project is not worth the money. It was necessary to do it more expensive, with good destructibility and different, not so reminiscent of a "Dog’s dream" scenario, or not to do at all.

As a long time XCOM fan, I was uncertain about the direction of The Bureau.  Here was a series that I loved with strong tactical strategy roots that had influenced the genre for nearly two decades... and it's newest release was going to be a third-person shooter.  I assumed that the game was a way to use the XCOM name to cash in on yet another Call of Duty clone.  Fast forward a couple of years and I realized that I was wrong.

The XCOM 2 announcement got me hyped up on the series once again and I decided that instead of playing through another war in XCOM: Enemy Within (which would've been a blast, even if it were my billionth war) I would try something new and actually give The Bureau a go.  It was a good decision.

The story in the game is enjoyable, though it gets a little weird and unexpectedly complicated toward the end.  Base building doesn't make an appearance in this game, however, there is an XCOM base where you spend your time in between missions and it is quite well done.  Different scenes play out as you wander through the base depending on events that you've experienced and choices that you've made.  For example, after defeating each new enemy type that you run across you can often see them being studied (in one way ot another) in your laboratory.

Combat, the meat and potatoes of this game, is significantly more fun than I had been assuming.  You issue commands to your squad mates (who come in Recon, Engineer, Support, and Soldier varieties) which include utilizing the abilities that they possess.  These squaddies level up and gain new abilities on a skill tree exclusive to each class that is reminiscent of XCOM: Enemy Unknown.  Two agents of the same class could use their abilities in different ways.

The feel of the combat itself reminds me of Mass Effect 2.  The cover system, the use of alien abilities (some which are very similar to biotics), and even the large variety of weapons to choose from in the game and their varying strengths and weaknesses.  However, it can not be overstated that the AI in this game is less than amazing.  You'll find yourself micromanaging your agents often as they can't seem to utilize themselves to be anywhere near as efficient as when you hold them by the hand and tell them what to do.  On a few occassions, I watched in horror as one of my agents moved away from an enemy grenade, only to realize that the best cover was were that grenade was and return to it to his imminent death.

All in all, this is a good game with plenty to offer that I recommend to XCOM fans and shooter/RPG fans alike.  As long as you can get past the AI it is a solid game with around a couple of dozen hours of content if you're playing on a difficulty level that challenges you.

The Bureau is a light tactical third-person shooter set in the 1960s' US when suddenly Earth becomes the target of an alien invasion. Of course a couple people suspected something like this may happen and formed The Bureau (aka XCOM) to at least deliver some resistance, and you end up being one of those designated to deliver some kickin' of butts to the alien invaders.

If you're familiar with the X-COM games of old, don't expect too much likeness - there are some elements from X-COM that have been incorporated into The Bureau, but overall it is noticeable that the game was meant to be something unrelated until halfway through development someone decided to slap the X-COM label on it. If you can look past the X-COM label (and, frankly, with the old X-COM games not really being overly heavy on story I believe this is not overly difficult), The Bureau is actually a fun and mostly well-designed TPS, playing very similar to the somewhat older Mass Effect games.

The game is very linear and relatively short, though - even if you want to make sure you see everything and read every snippet of in-game lore you'll beat the game (including the short second campaign available as DLC) in less than 20 hours. I don't think that's a bad thing, however - while the setting could certainly have been expanded on some more, I do appreciate a game that can actually be finished with 100% achievements in a reasonable amount of time.

Story-wise The Bureau is pretty decent, though parts of the story feel a bit too hurried and the meta twist at the end is rather contrived. Still, it is noticeable that a substantial amount of work has gone into the setting and at least I found it rather delightful to explore. I would have appreciated a less impulsive protagonist, though, and some of his flipping out in dialogues seems over the top to me.

Nevertheless, I think overall The Bureau very well accomplishes what it sets out to do, and at least to me it is one of the more entertaining games I have played recently. It is certainly not free of flaws, from repetitive face textures over somewhat too sticky cover impeding on your movement to a sometimes seriously handicapped companion AI, but I still feel that I can recommend it, at least to people who can enjoy story-driven tactical TPS games and don't take offense at the X-COM brand being slapped on a 1960s UFO conspiracy story.

The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is the second of the third-person shooter style game within the history of the series, which primarily takes on a top-down strategy style approach. The first title that took on a third-person shooter perspective was 2001's XCOM: Enforcer, which received mix reviews from fans and critics alike. Like all XCOM games before it, Declassified was published by 2K Games, but developed by 2K Marin instead of MicroProse Software, Inc., or any of the companies that worked on the Enemy Within release.

I'm not going to pretend to be some sort of XCOM enthusiast or expert, as I'm neither of those things; in fact, The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is the first title in the series that I've ever played. With that out of the way, you can guarantee this review will not be pining over the fact that this release isn't of the same gameplay style of say, UFO Defense or Enemy Unknown. Even though this is the second of the third-person shooter XCOM titles, it's a great refresher of the franchise in general, and it has the potential to reel gamers into the XCOM universe who may not be so crazy over top-down strategy games. As I was playing, I never once felt like I was out of the loop when it came to plot, in all reality it actually felt like I was starting at the beginning of the story.

It's 1962, and you're Agent William Carter; a man who has some deep demons to face from his past, but who is also an excellent operative. You've been assigned to XCOM, a top-secret government organization that by all official accounts does not exist. It's your job to take out the alien scum, or "Outsiders", that are invading the United States, and possibly the world; their reach is unknown, as all communications outside of the immediate area have been blacked out. There are some survivors that have been infected by the Outsiders, known as Sleepwalkers, and it's your hope that a cure will be found for them. You and your crew must find a way to ensure that humanity prevails, and depending on your decisions it may cost a lot to do so. Be prepared to take on some of the most dangerous alien elites.

Without a doubt, this game is a definite merger of Mass Effect and Gears of War. Its primary combat system relies heavily on cover-based shooting, and even on the easiest difficulty if you do not make use of cover... you will die. Despite the third-person shooter aspect of XCOM Declassified, there is still a tactical influence that will make your gameplay experience a whole lot easier if you utilize it. You are able to bring two other agents on missions with you, and you can fully command them on the battle field; you can tell them where to move to, which foe to shoot at, and also make them use their unique skills which will come in very helpful at times. There are four types of agents that you can choose between, all of which have their own benefits and skills that will come in handy during the numerous Outsider onslaughts. New skills are unlocked as the agents, and yourself, rank up by earning kills in combat. However, it's an unfortunate downside that the agent AI in this game is mediocre at best, and if you do not keep your commands on them at all times, their helpfulness is extremely low.

The Mass Effect influence comes in to play via dialogue choices, and even the dialogue system itself. Once you complete a major or minor mission, you will return to the central XCOM hub where you are able to interact with certain characters. Generally, you will also have three dialogue options to talk about to any given person. Talking to them will reveal much more of the storyline and backgrounds, and many of the choices that you make will have an affect on the ending that you will receive; in total, there are seven different endings. There are also letters, photographs, and recordings that you can pick up throughout the game; while they aren't required for any advancement or achievements, they do add further depth to the story that helps bring everything together.

While the story is extremely well written and exceptionally executed, so long as you take the time to talk to people and review letters and recordings, XCOM Declassified really shines when it comes to overall atmosphere. The environments are lavishly detailed, and no two mission areas are alike. Hands down, even though the game is dated by three years now, this is one of the best looking titles that I've ever had the pleasure of laying my eyes on. Between the fog effects, dynamic lighting, the clashing range of soft pastel colors and cold metallic alien structures, and spectacular recreation of a 1960's environment, there's absolutely no denying that this release is a visual stunner. All of it is wrapped together with an equally amazing soundtrack that will keep you engaged from beginning to end.

There is an unfortunate downside to XCOM Declassified that has resulted in the largest amount of its negative reviews. The controls are fairly unpolished and convoluted, while they could've followed the formula of so many other titles of the same vein. The worst of all is how hard it is to aim, even if you set the controller and/or mouse sensitivity very low, if you nudge in the same direction for even a fraction of a second too long, you overshoot your target and end up missing your mark entirely. This happens more often than not, and causes a lot of ammo to be wasted; which is unacceptable in an environment that requires some moderate resource management.

However, given the utterly brilliant storyline, jaw dropping landscapes, immersive atmosphere, superb optimization (60+ FPS at all times), and the huge bang you'll get for your buck (13-15 hours of play time), it's easy to forgive the control flaws as you will become so engrossed in everything that's going on around you that you'll just... what's the famous XCOM term?... Adapt. Survive. Win. If you're looking for a long lasting, totally immersive third-person shooter experience that has a story and visuals that you won't soon forget, The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is a must have for your Steam library. It'll leave you wanting more, and luckily there's some DLC for that.

The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is a game caught between two worlds, and it shows. From the very beginning, it presents a concept with undeniable intrigue: a tactical third-person shooter set during the height of Cold War paranoia, reimagining the origins of the XCOM organization amid a secret alien invasion in 1962. This backdrop is more than just aesthetic dressing—it becomes the game's strongest asset. The art direction leans heavily into period authenticity, with diners, government bunkers, small-town suburbs, and military installations painted in saturated mid-century tones. Radios hum with era-specific broadcasts, typewriters clack in dimly lit offices, and the early stages of America’s technological and political anxiety are palpable in every scene. This grounding in retro Americana infused with science fiction lends the game a unique identity that helps it stand apart visually, even when the mechanics struggle to match the same level of polish.

Where The Bureau starts to show cracks is in its gameplay. The core experience is a third-person shooter with tactical elements—essentially, a hybrid between Mass Effect's squad control and XCOM’s high-level strategy, but without the refinement of either. The game encourages you to pause combat using a radial menu called “Battle Focus,” from which you issue commands to your two AI-controlled teammates. These squadmates come in various classes—engineer, recon, support, and commando—each with its own skill tree and battlefield abilities. The idea is solid in theory: combine real-time shooting with tactical decision-making. In practice, though, the system is bogged down by AI inconsistencies, clunky interface design, and the constant need to micromanage underperforming allies. Instead of feeling like a capable field commander, you often feel like a babysitter, struggling to keep your squad alive rather than orchestrating complex strategies.

The combat encounters themselves are uneven. Early missions tease the potential of the system with some tense engagements and decent pacing. However, the repetitive enemy types, predictable patterns, and limited tactical variety eventually cause battles to blur together. There’s a loop that grows stale far too quickly: enter an area, set up cover, deploy a turret, issue a few commands, repeat. It doesn’t help that the enemy AI behaves erratically—sometimes overly aggressive, other times passively waiting for you to dispatch them one by one. As a result, firefights lack the kind of urgency or creativity that games like XCOM: Enemy Unknown or Mass Effect 2 handled so well. The lack of permanent death for agents (outside of optional difficulty settings) further removes any tension that might have made you care about your squadmates. They’re disposable in more ways than one—not just in gameplay, but narratively too.

The story, despite its strong setting, is a missed opportunity. You play as Agent William Carter, a brooding, emotionally wounded operative burdened with a mysterious past and a knack for yelling at subordinates. Unfortunately, Carter lacks the charisma or emotional complexity to carry the narrative, and most of the supporting cast is similarly underdeveloped. The dialogue system offers choices that occasionally affect the outcome of missions, but these moments feel superficial and rarely influence the overarching plot in meaningful ways. While there’s an attempt to weave in mystery and intrigue—complete with a twist involving consciousness transfer and alien manipulation—the game never fully earns its more ambitious narrative beats. The emotional stakes feel hollow, not because the story lacks big ideas, but because it fails to ground them in characters we care about.

That said, The Bureau does manage to deliver occasional moments of genuine atmosphere. The base hub—XCOM’s early command center—is dense with period detail, and wandering through its halls, eavesdropping on scientists and military personnel, can be surprisingly immersive. There's a sense of mounting dread as the alien threat escalates, and the game’s use of environmental storytelling does a decent job of reinforcing that feeling. Audio logs, newspaper clippings, and overheard conversations help flesh out the world in ways the main story fails to do. These quieter moments, oddly enough, often feel more engaging than the action sequences themselves.

Technically, the game runs smoothly on modern systems, though its visual fidelity has not aged particularly well. Character animations are stiff, facial expressions are wooden, and some textures are noticeably flat. The voice acting is serviceable, but rarely exceptional, and the soundtrack—while fitting for the tone—fails to leave much of a lasting impression. There are also a handful of bugs and glitches, though nothing game-breaking. It’s clear that this was a game with an ambitious scope but perhaps not the time, resources, or clarity of vision to fully realize its potential.

In the end, The Bureau: XCOM Declassified is a flawed but fascinating experiment. It tries to reimagine XCOM through the lens of a story-driven shooter while still holding onto its tactical roots, and in doing so, ends up pleasing few. For fans of the XCOM franchise, it lacks the strategic depth and emergent storytelling that defines the series. For shooter fans, the gunplay and squad mechanics feel sluggish and constrained. And for those drawn by the premise and setting, the thin character work and uneven pacing may prove disappointing. Yet for all its shortcomings, there is something admirable about its ambition. The Bureau doesn’t quite succeed in what it sets out to do, but it’s hard to ignore the charm in what it tries. It's the kind of game that some players might love in spite of itself—a misfire, yes, but an interesting one.

Described by TotalBiscuit as a mixture of Mass Effect and XCOM, The Bureau sees you fill the role of Agent Carter in a narrative prequel to Enemy Unknown and plays much as you would imagine a blend of those two games would, i.e. a tactical (mostly) third-person shooter set in the early XCOM universe. As Carter, you proceed from a surprise invasion through a story of intrigue up to a challenging final encounter, which (I believe) sets the scene well for the following games.

As you progress, you gain new abilities (really lite RPG) which either enhance or add new abilities. It is important to note that the skill tree (this applies to your squad as well) is a binary choice, i.e. you choose a skill following which the other option is locked permanently. Characterisation and voice acting are well done (with Carter deserving special mention) and the gameplay itself introduces new enemies on a fairly regular basis - even if everything does become repetitive after a while. You command two agents in addition to yourself - the agents all have their own specialities spread across four distinct classes and their skill trees are also assigned by the player, which adds a great deal of flexibility to the missions in terms of how you approach the situation.

However, one of the biggest issues with this game is the AI. Enemies can be a bit dense, but that is easily dealt with by just increasing the difficulty. Your squad mates are the real issue: expect to do a fair amount of micromanaging and brace for the resulting frustration. On lower difficulties it is not so bad, but on Commander it turns challenging scenarios into battles which are almost impossible to win: your squad mates will quite literally decide, all by themselves, that it is a good idea to change positions and run through enemy fire to do so. If one of them is downed, there is a short revive/stabilise period, but death is permanent  - if you lose a squad member, he will need to be replaced with another (most likely level 1 agent).

It is not the greatest game ever, and hardcore fans of the newer XCOM games might not find this to their taste - but there is some enjoyment here if you look for it with an open mind (assuming you can look past the shoddy AI). The game does feel like it could have benefited from another few weeks of QA, but it is not as bad as most people suggest.

Short version: I quite enjoyed this game despite its mixed reviews; I would recommend it to anyone who's a fan of the XCOM franchise [i]and[/i] third-person shooter games.

Short, short version: Is good game.  You buy.

Longer version: When I bought this game I went into it noting the 'Mixed' status and numerous less-than-enthusiastic reviews, thinking it to be one of those games I could ignore for a while and then install and play when I was bored enough.  In fact I played through a number of other games before getting to it.

I was surprised to find it both engaging and enjoyable.  A few people have said it has certain... [i]similarities[/i], shall we say, to the Mass Effect series and I'd have to agree.  It's a cover-based 3PS which involves a lot of hitting Space and going into slo-mo, issuing orders and flanking enemies.  It also has a radial conversation menu and various forms of pseudo-magical technology (most pertinently telekinesis and mind control).  Not only that but one of the squadmates' voices is done by Brandon Keener, who voiced Mass Effect's inestimable Garrus Vakarian (and he's not the only one; Courtenay Taylor, who voiced Angela Weaver in this game, also voiced Jack in the ME series - and there are plenty of others).  So that was nice.

From a story perspective it has plenty of depth [i]for what it is:[/i] a 60s themed alien invasion game.  This isn't Shakespeare and there's no point expecting it to be.  The whole story is based around giving you excuses to go out and shoot aliens and really, isn't that what you bought the game for?

What the story [i]doesn't[/i] have is complexity.  Don't bother looking for interpersonal nuances in this one because the conversation choices [i]at most[/i] boil down to 'be nice' and 'be an a-hole,' with no difference in the outcome.

You can't choose your character - or, at least, you can't at first.  You play through most of the game as Agent William Carter, a generic gravelly-voiced white dude with a tragic backstory who at least lacks stubble.  Later in the game you get to make a choice between playing for a little as one of three other characters but there's no character creation (or, for that matter, character development) in this one.

The landscape is pleasing to me.  Sometimes you're in town, at other times you're in the middle of alien bases.  Sometimes it's both.  Wherever you are, though, the art style remains recognisably XCOM.  Running through alien architecture at eye level where normally you'd be directing a squad from above is definitely a novel approach.

The UI is a little cumbersome at times but, having said that, I'm not entirely sure how I'd recommend the developers could have done it differently.  It works, it gets you through the game and it's not enough to drag you out of the game so hey, I could handle it.

Mechanics are very simplfied in some ways - there is no research or XCOM base inventory, for example.  You pick up a weapon, you collect it for use by anyone in your squad who's trained to use that item type (anyone skilled in pistol use can wield a plasma pistol, for example, even if you've only ever picked up one of them).  There's no armour (though you can wear 'backpacks' and some of them do indeed reduce enemy damage).

And this is the point: The Bureau is [i]not[/i] like other games in the XCOM series and some people find that jarring.  If you want turn-based squad mechanics with research, base inventories and other stuff like that, go to a different XCOM game (or wait for XCOM2).  This is not what you're looking for.  This is something different.

If, however, you're happy to play a 3PS game set in the same universe (if much earlier) with a story that doesn't require you to make notes on what choices you've made, this is a good one.

This game takes the tactical, high-stakes gameplay of XCOM and throws it into a very standard third-person cover shooter with squad commands. The result? A game that isn’t terrible, but also doesn’t stand out in any way.

The biggest issue is how dated and generic the gameplay feels. If you’ve played any cover-based shooter from the late 2000s to early 2010s (Mass Effect, Gears of War, etc.), you’ve played this. The shooting is serviceable but lacks impact, and the squad mechanics, while functional, never feel as deep or rewarding as XCOM’s turn-based strategy. The AI is also spotty—both for allies and enemies—making some encounters feel more frustrating than challenging.

That said, the game’s story and setting are decent. The Cold War-era alien invasion backdrop is a cool concept, and there’s an effort to blend noir and sci-fi that gives it some personality. The narrative has some interesting moments, even if it doesn’t fully stick the landing. The problem is that the actual gameplay rarely matches the intrigue of the premise.

Overall, The Bureau is a very by-the-numbers third-person shooter with a bit of XCOM flavor. If you’re a hardcore fan of the franchise, it’s an interesting curiosity, but don’t expect anything close to the depth or replayability of the main series.
